brave-llmcontext.snippet:
Scale: 1,067 sessions · 53,362 attributed contributions (47,290 spoken in the chamber, 6,072 submitted in writing) · 2,473 identified persons · 76 years of proceedings Why this chamber is different The Bundesrat is not a second elected chamber. Its members are delegates of the sixteen Land governments, appointed and recallable by them. Article 51(3) of the Basic Law requires each Land to cast its votes einheitlich as a bloc and the chamber has no Fraktionen (no party affiliations).
There is therefore no party field, and its absence is a design decision rather than a gap: the operative political unit is territorial. Every contribution carries the Bundesland it was made for, which makes territorial representation and federal–state conflict directly measurable from text. The chamber is also permanent, never dissolved, no elections, continuous session numbering since 1949 so the corpus is a single unbroken series rather than one segmented by legislative period.
Dataset files speeches.parquet, one row per attributed contribution by a named member: speaker name, resolved person_id, role, Bundesland, full German text, and contribution_type marking whether it was spoken in the chamber or submitted to the record in writing (102 MB). Gender is not stored here; join persons.parquet on person_id. persons.parquet, one row per resolved individual: canonical name, all name variants merged, career span, modal role and Bundesland, gender. Use this, not speakers.parquet, for person-level analysis.
sessions.parquet, one row per sitting: date, meeting city, extraction engine, source PDF hash, presiding_land (the Land holding the rotating annual presidency), and separate counts of spoken and written contributions. speakers.parquet, name-string index: one row per unique name string as extracted. # The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
## 1 Background & Summary
To address the aforementioned data gap, in this Data Descriptor, we present a complete speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber’s first sitting on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. It comprises 53,362 speeches delivered in the chamber including written statements.
## 2 Methods
### 2.2 Data Source
It is published in different period-based web pages (e.g., 1949–1950, 1951–1955, …, 2026–2030) as PDF documents. Each PDF document represents one session and the filename carries useful information, including session number and date that are essential for building the metadata. The corpus is designed to be extensible; thus, newer sessions can be added accordingly.
## 3 Data Records
### 3.1 Dataset Overview
The dataset contains four tables built from 1,067 per session attribution files and the extraction catalog by a packaging step that performs no parsing of its own. Every field in the corpus is either carried from the attribution files or computed by aggregation so the package can be built at any time without disturbing the speech layer.
All text fields are UTF-8 encoded, null values are represented as null in Parquet and as empty strings in the CSV file. The dataset is publicly available on Zenodo https://zenodo.org/records/22086439 under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC BY4.0).

Structured, speaker-attributed corpus of all German Bundesrat (Federal Council) plenary session transcripts (Plenarprotokolle) from the chamber's first sitting to the present (sessions 1–1067, September 1949 – July 2026). Why this chamber is different

The Bundesrat is not a second elected chamber. Its members are delegates of the sixteen Land governments, appointed and recallable by them. Article 51(3) of the Basic Law requires each Land to cast its votes einheitlich as a bloc and the chamber has no Fraktionen (no party affiliations). There is therefore no party field, and its absence is a design decision rather than a gap: the operative political unit is territorial. Every contribution carries the Bundesland it was made for, which makes territorial representation and federal–state conflict directly measurable from text.

The chamber is also permanent, never dissolved, no elections, continuous session numbering since 1949 so the corpus is a single unbroken series rather than one segmented by legislative period.

Overviews of the agendas ( Tagesordnungen ) for the current and last two plenary sessions contain an enumeration of the agenda points with the relevant official documents, These overviews also indicate which committees examined the proposals and list speakers registered for speaking time on the various agenda points. The stenographic reports ( Plenarprotokolle ) contain a verbatim report of all comments during the plenary sessions. All stenographic reports since 2000 can be consulted online.

Information about the Bundesrat's work and how it participates in the legislative process is also available in the form of various statistical evaluations.

The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system.
The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments.
Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available.
To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026.
In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements.
Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender.
The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.

The Bundesrat is the chamber representing the states of the Federal Republic of Germany, based in Berlin. It consists of 69 delegates from the 16 federal states, with each state holding a different number of votes depending on the size of its population.

The institution was created in 1949 through the Basic Law after the Second World War as a constitutional organ of the new Federal Republic. It drew on older forms of federal representation that had existed in Germany since the 19th century.

The Bundesrat meets in the former Prussian House of Lords, where modern democracy now occupies rooms once used by aristocrats. The building reminds visitors how political power has shifted over generations, turning an old chamber of privilege into a working federal institution.

Voting strength ranges from three to six votes per state, giving smaller regions a stronger voice relative to their population. This arrangement ensures that all regions can influence federal legislation, regardless of their size.

# The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council

### Authors/Creators

- Njie, Adama 1 
- Laperne, Leandro
- Agarwal, Laksh
- Torkayesh, Ali 1, 2 
- Venghaus, Sandra 1, 2 

## Description

Structured, speaker-attributed corpus of all German Bundesrat (Federal Council) plenary session transcripts (Plenarprotokolle) from the chamber's first sitting to the present (sessions 1–1067, September 1949 – July 2026). Every attributed contribution is extracted from the official PDFs published by the Bundesrat and linked to the speaker's name, resolved person identity, official role, gender, and Bundesland (Federal State) the speaker represents.

Scale: 1,067 sessions · 53,362 attributed contributions (47,290 spoken in the chamber, 6,072 submitted in writing) · 2,473 identified persons · 76 years of proceedings

Why this chamber is different

The Bundesrat is not a second elected chamber. Its members are delegates of the sixteen Land governments, appointed and recallable by them. Article 51(3) of the Basic Law requires each Land to cast its votes einheitlich as a bloc and the chamber has no Fraktionen (no party affiliations). There is therefore no party field, and its absence is a design decision rather than a gap: the operative political unit is territorial. Every contribution carries the Bundesland it was made for, which makes territorial representation and federal–state conflict directly measurable from text.

The chamber is also permanent, never dissolved, no elections, continuous session numbering since 1949 so the corpus is a single unbroken series rather than one segmented by legislative period.

# The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
## 1 Background & Summary
To address the aforementioned data gap, in this Data Descriptor, we present a complete speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber’s first sitting on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. It comprises 53,362 speeches delivered in the chamber including written statements.
## 2 Methods
### 2.2 Data Source
It is published in different period-based web pages (e.g., 1949–1950, 1951–1955, …, 2026–2030) as PDF documents. Each PDF document represents one session and the filename carries useful information, including session number and date that are essential for building the metadata. The corpus is designed to be extensible; thus, newer sessions can be added accordingly.
## 3 Data Records
### 3.1 Dataset Overview
The dataset contains four tables built from 1,067 per session attribution files and the extraction catalog by a packaging step that performs no parsing of its own. Every field in the corpus is either carried from the attribution files or computed by aggregation so the package can be built at any time without disturbing the speech layer.
All text fields are UTF-8 encoded, null values are represented as null in Parquet and as empty strings in the CSV file. The dataset is publicly available on Zenodo https://zenodo.org/records/22086439 under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC BY4.0).

webiq.snippet:
Am 7. März 2026 öffnete es erstmals seine Magazine und präsentierte sich und seine Arbeit am „Tag der Archive“ einer interessierten Öffentlichkeit.

Das Archiv des Bundesrates fungiert als sein historisches Gedächtnis und soll mit seinen Inhalten das politische Handeln des Verfassungsorgans für künftige Generationen nachvollziehbar machen. Der Archivbestand umfasst unter anderem Schriftgut (Akten, Drucksachen, Protokolle) sowie Ton- und Videoaufzeichnungen von Plenar- und Ausschusssitzungen und anderen ausgewählten parlamentarischen Veranstaltungen. Außerdem existiert ein Fotoarchiv. Dieser „Informationsspeicher“ beinhaltet Archivgut ab dem Jahr 1949, bei den analogen Fotos setzt die Überlieferung bereits 1936 ein. ... Um den direkten Zugriff auf die eigenen Archivalien zu haben, entschied sich der Bundesrat bereits im Jahr 1970 für ein eigenes Archiv. Die Mitarbeiterinnen und Mitarbeiter bewerten angebotene Akten der Ausschüsse und Arbeitsbereiche auf Archivwürdigkeit, um sie in diesem Fall zu übernehmen und für die Zukunft zu sichern. Im Anschluss erschließen sie die enthaltenen Informationen und stellen sie in speziellen Datenbanken bereit.

Der Umfang der Archivbestände beträgt derzeit ca. 2.000 Regalmeter, wächst im Zuge der Digitalisierung allerdings nicht mehr so stark an, wie noch vor einigen Jahren.
